central_question: How do logarithms express unknown exponents, simplify multiplicative calculations, model logarithmic scales, and solve equations while respecting their domain?

known_pitfalls.claim: log_b a means b divided by a.
known_pitfalls.correction: log_b a is the exponent x for which b^x = a.

known_pitfalls.claim: A logarithm can have any real base.
known_pitfalls.correction: For real logarithms, the base must satisfy b > 0 and b ≠ 1.

known_pitfalls.claim: The argument of a real logarithm may be zero or negative.
known_pitfalls.correction: The argument must be strictly positive; log_b 0 and log_b of a negative number are not defined in the real number system.

known_pitfalls.claim: log_a(M + N) = log_a M + log_a N.
known_pitfalls.correction: The product rule applies to multiplication, not addition: log_a(MN) = log_a M + log_a N.

known_pitfalls.claim: log_a(M − N) = log_a M − log_a N.
known_pitfalls.correction: The quotient rule applies to division: log_a(M/N) = log_a M − log_a N; there is no corresponding subtraction rule.
The exponent comes down as a multiplier: log_a(M^k) = k log_a M.

known_pitfalls.claim: When no base is written, log always means natural logarithm.
known_pitfalls.correction: In this chapter, log x without a written base denotes the common logarithm log_10 x, while ln x denotes log_e x.

known_pitfalls.claim: Every algebraic root obtained while solving a logarithmic equation is valid.
known_pitfalls.correction: Each candidate must be checked in the original equation; any value making a logarithmic argument zero or negative is an extraneous root.

known_pitfalls.claim: A difference of 3 on a base-10 logarithmic scale represents a factor of 3.
known_pitfalls.correction: A difference of 3 corresponds to a ratio of 10^3 = 1000 in the underlying quantity described by that scale.

recommended_example_progression: Use the Opening Puzzle and Examples 1-2 to connect powers with logarithms and convert between the two forms.
Use Exercise 2.1 to practise positive, zero, negative, and fractional exponents in logarithmic notation.
Use Example 3 to combine sums and differences of logarithms into one logarithm.
Use Examples 4-5 to evaluate exact logarithms by rewriting arguments as powers of the base.
Use Examples 6-8 and Exercise 2.2 to work with common logarithms, symbolic values, and constants rewritten as logarithms.
Use Example 9 and Exercise 2.3 Question 5 to interpret base-10 differences on earthquake, pH, and brightness scales.
Use Example 10 to solve a one-logarithm linear equation and check its domain.
Use Example 11 to combine logarithms, solve a quadratic, and reject an extraneous root.
Use Example 12 to show that a negative value of x can still be valid when the logarithmic argument remains positive.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The chapter provides Exercise 2.1, Exercise 2.2, and Exercise 2.3, followed by solved logarithmic-equation Examples 10-12.

beyond_the_textbook: Computer algorithms are often analysed using logarithms because repeatedly halving a problem leads to a number of steps proportional to log_2 of the input size.
Astronomers use logarithmic magnitude scales to compare objects whose brightnesses span extremely large ratios.
Information theory measures information in bits using base-2 logarithms because each binary choice has two possible outcomes.
The natural logarithm appears whenever a continuously growing or decaying quantity is modelled mathematically, including idealised population, cooling, and radioactive-decay models.
A logarithmic graph can reveal multiplicative patterns that are difficult to see on an ordinary linear axis.
